tagline: Art deco capital above the Red Sea
overview:
Eritrea stretches along the southwestern shore of the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa, about the size of Pennsylvania, with Sudan to the north, Ethiopia to the south, and Djibouti at its tip. Its name comes from the ancient Greek word for the Red Sea. The capital, Asmara, sits on a cool highland plateau at 2,300 meters and is famous for hundreds of art deco buildings from the 1930s, including a gas station shaped like an airplane, which earned it a place on UNESCO's World Heritage list.

Roughly 3.5 to 6 million people live in Eritrea; no census has been taken in decades, so estimates vary widely. Tigrinya, Arabic, and English are the working languages, and nine ethnic groups speak their own tongues. About half the population is Christian and half Muslim. Eritrea won independence from Ethiopia in 1993 after a 30-year war, and the same president has governed ever since without elections. Most people farm or herd, and many young Eritreans have left the country, partly because of a long national service requirement.
landAndNature: Eritrea climbs from one of the hottest coasts on Earth to cool green highlands in just 100 kilometers. The Danakil Depression in the south lies more than 100 meters below sea level and is a furnace of salt flats and volcanic vents. The central highlands, part of the Ethiopian plateau, have terraced fields and a mild climate, with Mount Soira reaching about 3,000 meters. To the west the land slopes down to the hot lowlands of the Gash and Barka rivers. Offshore, the Dahlak Archipelago has more than 100 islands with pristine coral reefs, dugongs, and dolphins. Elephants survive in the southwest near Gash-Setit, and the country is one of the last places where wild African asses roam.
peopleAndCulture: The Tigrinya are the largest group, followed by the Tigre, Saho, Afar, Bilen, Kunama, Nara, Rashaida, and Hedareb. Meals are shared from a single platter: injera, a spongy sourdough flatbread, is torn by hand and used to scoop up spicy stews called tsebhi. Coffee is roasted, ground, and served in a slow ceremony with popcorn. Italy's colonial years left a taste for pasta, espresso, and gelato, and Asmara's cafés serve cappuccino beside traditional coffee. Cycling is the national sport; Eritreans are the strongest cyclists in Africa and have raced in the Tour de France, and huge crowds line the roads for races. Orthodox Christian festivals like Timket and Muslim holidays are both national celebrations.
history: The region was part of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum, which traded across the Red Sea and adopted Christianity in the 300s; the port of Adulis was its gateway. Ottoman and Egyptian rulers later held the coast. Italy made Eritrea a colony in 1890, built Asmara's railway and modern buildings, and used it as a base to invade Ethiopia in 1935. Britain took over in 1941, and in 1952 Eritrea was joined to Ethiopia in a federation that Ethiopia soon dissolved. A war for independence began in 1961 and lasted 30 years until Eritrean fighters won in 1991, followed by an independence vote in 1993. A border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000 killed tens of thousands. A peace agreement was finally signed in 2018.
funFacts: Asmara's Fiat Tagliero building, finished in 1938, is a gas station designed to look like an airplane with 30-meter concrete wings.
A steam railway built by Italy still climbs from the coast to Asmara, rising 2,300 meters through 30 tunnels.
Eritrea has one of the strongest cycling traditions in Africa, and Daniel Teklehaimanot wore the King of the Mountains jersey at the 2015 Tour de France.
The name Eritrea comes from Erythra Thalassa, the ancient Greek name for the Red Sea.
The Dahlak Archipelago has more than 100 islands, but only a handful have any people living on them.
